questions.prompt: Stage 1's drain sits at 1.0 V DC; stage 2 needs its gate at 0.7 V DC. Why is a direct wire a problem?
options: A wire cannot carry the signal
The wire forces stage 2's gate to 1.0 V, so its bias is set by stage 1, not by its own design
The wire adds noise
It would shift stage 1's gain to zero
questions.explanation: Direct (DC) coupling makes the two bias points interdependent; here stage 2 would run at a much larger \(V_{ov}\) than intended (reader Sec. 12.2).

questions.prompt: How does an ideal coupling capacitor behave?
options: Short at DC, open at signal frequencies
A resistor at all frequencies
Open at DC, nearly a short at the signal frequencies
Open at all frequencies
questions.explanation: \(Z = 1/(j\omega C)\): infinite at DC (bias points stay isolated), small when \(\omega C\) is large (the signal passes).

questions.prompt: A gate bias divider has \(R_1 = 300\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) from \(V_{DD} = 1.8\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(R_2 = 150\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) to ground; the signal arrives through a coupling capacitor from a source with 1 V DC offset. Find the gate's DC voltage in V.
questions.explanation: The capacitor blocks the source's DC, so only the divider sets the gate: \(1.8\cdot150/450 = 0.6\ \mathrm{V}\). Including the 1 V offset would be the mistake the capacitor prevents.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of AC coupling in an integrated circuit?
options: It makes bias points interdependent
It adds DC gain
It requires a negative supply
It cannot pass DC or very low frequencies, and the large capacitors it needs take lots of area
questions.explanation: Large on-chip capacitors are costly, and some signals (sensors, op-amp inputs) include DC. That is why IC amplifiers are mostly DC coupled.

questions.prompt: Stages are DC coupled: stage 1's drain drives stage 2's gate, which needs 0.75 V. With \(V_{DD} = 1.8\ \mathrm{V}\) and stage 1 drawing \(150\ \mu\mathrm{A}\), what \(R_{D1}\) (in kΩ) sets this level?
questions.explanation: \(V_{D1} = V_{DD} - I_DR_{D1} = 0.75\): \(R_{D1} = 1.05/150\ \mu\mathrm{A} = 7\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). With DC coupling, stage 1's design is constrained by stage 2's bias.

questions.prompt: A large capacitor is placed across a source resistor \(R_S\). What does it achieve?
options: \(R_S\) still sets the DC bias, but the source is at AC ground for signals
It removes \(R_S\) from the DC bias
It raises the DC source voltage
It blocks the signal from reaching the drain
questions.explanation: A bypass capacitor is the same isolation idea: open at DC (bias uses \(R_S\)), short at signal frequencies.

questions.prompt: Gate divider \(R_1 = 1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\) from \(V_{DD} = 2.5\ \mathrm{V}\), \(R_2 = 470\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) to ground; the source (50 Ω, 0.3 V DC) connects through a coupling capacitor. Gate DC voltage in V?
questions.explanation: \(2.5\cdot470/1470 \approx 0.799\ \mathrm{V}\). The source's 50 Ω and its 0.3 V are both isolated by the capacitor at DC.

questions.prompt: In a three-stage DC-coupled amplifier, stage 1's drain drifts up 20 mV with temperature. What happens downstream?
options: Nothing; later stages have their own bias
The drift is amplified by later stages like a signal and can push them out of saturation
It is cancelled automatically
Only stage 1 is affected
questions.explanation: With DC coupling a bias shift is indistinguishable from a slow input. This is why DC-coupled chains use differential stages and feedback to fix the operating points.

questions.prompt: Which choice gives the most independent bias design for each stage?
options: DC coupling with matched stages
DC coupling with larger resistors
AC coupling between stages, each with its own bias network
Removing the bias networks
questions.explanation: Capacitors make each stage's DC operating point independent; the price is low-frequency response and area.

questions.prompt: Preview of low-frequency response: a coupling capacitor feeding a bias network's resistance forms what kind of filter?
options: A low-pass filter
An all-pass filter
A notch filter
A high-pass filter, so very low frequencies are attenuated
questions.explanation: Series \(C\) into a shunt \(R\): gain rises from 0 at DC to 1 above \(1/(2\pi RC)\).

questions.prompt: Preview of the differential pair: why do DC-coupled IC amplifiers favour differential stages?
options: A common shift on both inputs (like bias drift) is largely rejected
They need no bias current
They have no output resistance
They block DC like a capacitor
questions.explanation: The pair responds to the difference of its inputs, so common DC errors largely cancel.
